verdicts.rewritten_summary: National-framework investigation (BuzzFeed, Rozenn Le Carboulec, published January 2018) on trans women in French prisons — the custody framework the record applies unchanged to this region: Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code places detainees by the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still legally marked male are held in all-male facilities; a trans woman from Argentina whose passport lists her as female spent three days in a men's facility in Lille amid inmate threats (an inmate tried to attack her with a knife), and another detainee was held after a 2016 Paris protest trial; as of 1 November 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees in France, and damages obtained for one detainee's detention conditions were a symbolic 2,000 euros. No Occitanie-specific event appears; the article supports the record's claim that this national custody framework applies in every department.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 by the national detention inspector-general (CGLPL), covering every place of deprivation of liberty and relevant to this region because its visits included the Toulouse-Seysses prison and the Toulouse central police station, with findings concerning eight transgender women held in those Toulouse facilities. Built on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons, it documents serious persisting violations — isolation imposed for trans status, staff untrained on trans issues, and the 2016 depathologisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) never written into prison rules or healthcare guidance — and recommends financing research, policies against discrimination, and suitable procedures for searching and assigning persons whose civil-status sex does not match their presented identity.

The Diplomat, 14 August 2026, national-repression analysis that the record's climate claims rest on: President Prabowo's October 2025 presidential decree listed "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among the country's non-military national-security threats (as reported in the Jakarta Post), and activists describe a post-decree wave of hate crimes — notably in Bogor (West Java), where over 15 trans women were doused with urine, forced to strip naked and beaten; the piece also documents editors killing LGBTQ+ stories for fear of reprisal, notes Indonesia lacks explicit anti-LGBTQ+ laws but has legal frameworks that indirectly discriminate, with same-sex activity criminalisable under moral laws and Aceh's syariah regime most conservative. No Jakarta-specific event appears in this source (the record's February 2025 hotel-raid claim is not covered here); the article supports the record's national-climate claims as the framework this region operates under.

National-framework HRW news release, 26 March 2026, on the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, which the record's national-backdrop paragraph relies on: the bill amends the 2019 law, removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender that HRW calls reminiscent of colonial-era provisions criminalising transgender persons for appearing dressed as women; India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security. No Maharashtra-specific content in this source (the record's Nagpur entry-screening claim is not covered here); the article supports the record's claim that this national framework applies in every state including Maharashtra.

National-framework BBC News article on the same 2026 amendment bill: approved by both houses and now needing presidential assent; it removes the right to self-identify, limiting recognition, in a reversal of the 2014 Supreme Court "third gender"/self-determination ruling; critics warn it could exclude many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people from welfare benefits, and lawyer N Kavitha Rameshwar called the medical-certification requirement an "attack on the privacy and dignity of the individual", while the government argues the narrower definition targets those facing "extreme and oppressive" discrimination and prevents exploitation and trafficking. No Maharashtra-specific content (the record's Nagpur/VHP/Aadhaar festival-screening claim is not covered by this source); the article supports the record's national-backdrop claims.

National-framework HRW news release, 26 March 2026 — core source for the record's claims: the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates "coercing or alluring" offences that could criminalise support systems; HRW calls it a major reversal of hard-won rights and urges the president not to sign it. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security — the national documentation gap the record concentrates in the capital. No Delhi-specific event in this source.

National-framework BBC News article on the 2026 amendment bill: approved by both houses and now awaiting presidential assent; it removes the right to self-identify in a reversal of the 2014 Supreme Court ruling; the record's capital-protest-politics claim is evidenced here — activist Grace Banu told a press conference in Delhi the community sought "recognition without invasion" and "rights without humiliation" — and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider amid privacy-and-dignity challenges. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protections against exploitation and trafficking.

Seoul-specific ruling coverage (Korea Times, 22 July 2024): the Seoul Central District Court (presiding judge Chung In-jae) dismissed the state's appeal and ruled partially for plaintiff A in a damages lawsuit against the state, awarding 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed; the decision became final on 2 July 2024 after neither party appealed, holding that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights — "the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right." Underpinning data: a 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 trans respondents found 41% used another-gender restrooms out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether; the piece also cites a 2021 Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court ruling of 7 million won damages against an academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

National judicial-framework item (Yonhap, 8 May 2024): the regional court in the central county of Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker change for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to one's gender identity; the national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them. The ruling is not from a capital court — it evidences the national judicial trend the record cites for Seoul, and no Seoul-specific source covers that claim.

National-progress HRW article (31 March 2025) with a state-by-state legal-gender-recognition table that includes this region: the Supreme Court laid out clear guidelines to states on legal gender recognition and extended the right to all children in 2022, the Inter-American Court found states are obliged to recognise gender identity, and states keep authority over civil/family/registration law — but only seven states extend legal gender recognition to children and some states still have no law or only procedure-in-practice; the table's Quintana Roo entry shows the state's congress passed its legal-gender-recognition statute in 2020, supporting the record's countervailing claim. The article also flags that for many trans people "any request for documents is fraught with the potential for discrimination, violence, and humiliation", directly relevant to the document screening a visitor faces. The record's Cancún/Tulum policing claims and the December 2023 conversion-practices ban are not covered in this source.

Malaysia country profile (Human Dignity Trust, last updated 16 December 2025) with both the national framework and Selangor-specific enforcement: Penal Code sections 377A-377D criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment with whipping (a law enforced in recent years; both men and women, and usable against trans people), and Sharia state enactments criminalise cross-dressing and "males posing as females"; Selangor-specific content — the Federal Court struck down provisions of Selangor's Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding state power (2021), the Selangor state authorities issued an arrest warrant for a trans businesswoman who failed to appear in court and announced the deployment of 122 religious-affairs officers (the Sajat case), and a Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane; at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community ongoing since the 2018 election.

HRW/Justice for Sisters report release (10 August 2022) documenting Malaysia's state-backed discrimination, including the Selangor episode the record leads with: in 2021 Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear in court in Selangor to answer criminal charges for "insulting Islam" based on her attire; the state's religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand — a deployment HRW/JFS cite as showing how far authorities go to enforce rigid gender norms (she was permitted to stay under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia). National framework context: the federal penal code punishes oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison, Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, investigations covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, and state "rehabilitation" programmes were found to internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred.

Malaysia country profile (Human Dignity Trust, last updated 16 December 2025) — the national-framework source the record's baseline rests on — with Johor-specific content: in November 2023 the Johor government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people, the record's one documented local divergence beyond the national baseline. The framework applied locally: Penal Code sections 377A-377D criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment with whipping for both men and women, Sharia enactments prohibit cross-dressing and "males posing as females", same-sex intimacy is also criminalised by state Sharia laws applying to Muslims, and at least 1,733 people had attended "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021 under a crackdown ongoing since the 2018 election.

National-framework HRW/Justice for Sisters report release (10 August 2022) supporting the record's claim that the national baseline applies unchanged in Johor and is enforced through state religious authorities: the federal penal code punishes oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison, Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, state-conducted investigations covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, and a crackdown on the LGBT community has run since the 2018 election. No Johor-specific incident appears in this source; the record's local finding (Johor's 2023 conversion-therapy-centre plans) is covered by the paired Human Dignity Trust profile.
